title: Security, Privacy & Permissions
scopeHtml: Scope: Keychain, biometrics, App Transport Security, permissions, privacy manifests, App Tracking Transparency, data protection, jailbreak.

notes.title: Baseline and the iOS security mindset
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. On Android you lean on the Keystore, EncryptedSharedPreferences/DataStore, BiometricPrompt, the network security config, runtime permissions and Play Integrity. On iOS the same jobs belong to the Keychain, Secure Enclave, LocalAuthentication, App Transport Security (ATS), Info.plist usage strings, privacy manifests and App Attest.

Baseline for every note in this track. Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 as the minimum target, SwiftUI-first with UIKit essentials. Modern APIs by default (@Observable, async/await, actors, Swift Testing, URLSession async). Legacy forms are labelled "old codebase". Anything new in iOS 18/26 is marked verify.

The iOS security model rests on four ideas:

  1. Sandbox. Every app runs in its own container directory and cannot read another app's files. There is no "external storage" free-for-all like pre-Android-10.
  2. Code signing. Only code signed by a certificate Apple trusts runs (see the signing note in this track). The kernel refuses unsigned pages.
  3. Entitlements. Powers such as Keychain sharing, push, App Groups and associated domains are declared in a signed .entitlements file. Apple's provisioning profile must grant them.
  4. Consent at the OS level. Sensitive data (camera, location, contacts, photos) sits behind a system prompt, and the answer is stored per app by the OS.
+-------------------- device --------------------+
|  Secure Enclave (own CPU, keys never leave)    |
|  Kernel: sandbox + signature check + entitle.  |
|  +--------------+   +--------------+           |
|  | App A        |   | App B        |           |
|  | container    |   | container    |           |
|  | Keychain item|   | Keychain item|  (items scoped by access group)
|  +--------------+   +--------------+           |
+------------------------------------------------+
Android iOS
Android Keystore Keychain Services + Secure Enclave keys
BiometricPrompt LocalAuthentication (LAContext)
network_security_config.xml ATS keys in Info.plist, URLSessionDelegate pinning
Manifest <uses-permission> + runtime request Info.plist usage string + system prompt on first use
Play Data safety form App Privacy labels + PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy
Play Integrity API App Attest / DeviceCheck
android:allowBackup iCloud/iTunes backup rules, isExcludedFromBackup

Real industry examples. Banking apps (Revolut, Monzo) keep tokens in the Keychain and gate sensitive actions with Face ID. 1Password builds on Keychain primitives plus Secure Enclave wrapped keys. Signal keeps its database key in the Keychain with a device-only accessibility class.

Everyday analogy. The sandbox is a hotel room: you have your own key, you cannot enter the next room, and the front desk (the OS) decides when you may use the gym (camera) or pool (location).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying iOS has no encryption at rest unless you add it. Data protection is on by default for new files in modern iOS (the default class is "complete until first user authentication"); you choose stricter classes.
  • Treating a missing Keystore as a gap: the Keychain is the equivalent and it is simpler to use.
  • Assuming a jailbroken or rooted check is a security boundary. It is only a speed bump (see the jailbreak section).

notes.title: Keychain services and accessibility classes
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. On Android you generate a key in the Keystore and encrypt blobs yourself, or use EncryptedSharedPreferences. On iOS the Keychain stores small secrets (tokens, passwords, keys) directly: you hand it bytes and it encrypts, persists and access-controls them.

Mechanism. The Keychain is an encrypted SQLite database managed by the securityd daemon, not by your process. Your app calls the C API in Security.framework (SecItemAdd, SecItemCopyMatching, SecItemUpdate, SecItemDelete) with a dictionary of attributes. An item's identity is defined by its class plus key attributes: for generic passwords (kSecClassGenericPassword) the pair kSecAttrService + kSecAttrAccount (plus the access group) forms the unique key. Adding a duplicate returns errSecDuplicateItem.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
import Security
import Foundation

enum KeychainError: Error { case status(OSStatus), notFound }

struct Keychain: Sendable {
    let service: String

    func save(_ data: Data, account: String) throws {
        let query: [String: Any] = [
            kSecClass as String: kSecClassGenericPassword,
            kSecAttrService as String: service,
            kSecAttrAccount as String: account,
            kSecAttrAccessible as String: kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly,
            kSecValueData as String: data
        ]
        var status = SecItemAdd(query as CFDictionary, nil)
        if status == errSecDuplicateItem {
            let match: [String: Any] = [
                kSecClass as String: kSecClassGenericPassword,
                kSecAttrService as String: service,
                kSecAttrAccount as String: account
            ]
            status = SecItemUpdate(match as CFDictionary,
                                   [kSecValueData as String: data] as CFDictionary)
        }
        guard status == errSecSuccess else { throw KeychainError.status(status) }
    }

    func load(account: String) throws -> Data {
        let query: [String: Any] = [
            kSecClass as String: kSecClassGenericPassword,
            kSecAttrService as String: service,
            kSecAttrAccount as String: account,
            kSecReturnData as String: true,
            kSecMatchLimit as String: kSecMatchLimitOne
        ]
        var result: AnyObject?
        let status = SecItemCopyMatching(query as CFDictionary, &result)
        if status == errSecItemNotFound { throw KeychainError.notFound }
        guard status == errSecSuccess, let data = result as? Data else {
            throw KeychainError.status(status)
        }
        return data
    }
}
// Android: EncryptedSharedPreferences (androidx.security:security-crypto)
val masterKey = MasterKey.Builder(context)
    .setKeyScheme(MasterKey.KeyScheme.AES256_GCM)
    .build()

val prefs = EncryptedSharedPreferences.create(
    context, "secrets", masterKey,
    EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefKeyEncryptionScheme.AES256_SIV,
    EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefValueEncryptionScheme.AES256_GCM
)
prefs.edit().putString("access_token", token).apply()
val token = prefs.getString("access_token", null)

Accessibility classes (kSecAttrAccessible). This decides when the item's decryption key is available.

Constant Readable when Typical use
...WhenUnlocked device unlocked passwords for foreground-only use
...AfterFirstUnlock after first unlock since boot tokens read by background fetch / push extensions
...WhenPasscodeSetThisDeviceOnly unlocked and passcode set highest-sensitivity secrets; deleted if passcode removed
...ThisDeviceOnly variants as above, but excluded from backup and device migration anything that must not leave the phone

The default, if you set nothing, is kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked. A background task that runs while the phone is locked then fails with errSecInteractionNotAllowed (-25308). This is the classic production bug: "token read works in debug, fails for users whose phone is locked in a pocket during background refresh". Fix: AfterFirstUnlock.

Access groups and sharing. Items belong to an access group (team ID prefix + bundle ID by default). Enable the Keychain Sharing capability to share between your own apps and extensions (share extension, notification service extension). Apps from different teams cannot share.

Survives reinstall? Keychain items are NOT deleted when the app is uninstalled (unlike Android's app data, wiped on uninstall). A new install can see the old token. Apps typically write a "first launch" flag in UserDefaults (which is wiped) and clear the Keychain when the flag is missing. Mixing this up causes either "user is still logged in after reinstall" bugs or silent re-auth.

Real industry examples. Auth0 and Firebase Auth SDKs persist refresh tokens in the Keychain. The KeychainAccess and Valet (Square) libraries wrap the raw API; Valet's value is a safe accessibility choice per instance. Use the raw API for one or two items; use a wrapper beyond that.

Everyday analogy. The Keychain is a bank safe-deposit room: you never hold the vault key (securityd does), you ask the clerk to put a box in or fetch it, and the box outlives your visit (reinstall).

Common interview traps.

  • Storing tokens in UserDefaults. It is a plain plist in the container, readable in an unencrypted backup or on a jailbroken device.
  • Forgetting ThisDeviceOnly, so secrets travel into backups and new devices.
  • Calling the Keychain API on the main thread in a hot path; it is an IPC to securityd and can block on first access after boot.
  • Assuming uninstall clears the Keychain.

notes.title: Face ID, Touch ID and LocalAuthentication
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. BiometricPrompt with a CryptoObject on Android; on iOS LAContext.evaluatePolicy. The crucial point is the same: a boolean "authenticated" is weak; binding a Keychain item to the biometric is strong.

The weak way (UI gate only).

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
import LocalAuthentication

func unlock() async -> Bool {
    let context = LAContext()
    var error: NSError?
    guard context.canEvaluatePolicy(.deviceOwnerAuthenticationWithBiometrics, error: &error) else {
        return false // no biometrics enrolled, or locked out
    }
    do {
        return try await context.evaluatePolicy(
            .deviceOwnerAuthenticationWithBiometrics,
            localizedReason: "Unlock your wallet")
    } catch {
        return false // user cancelled, failed, or lockout
    }
}
val prompt = BiometricPrompt(activity, executor,
    object : BiometricPrompt.AuthenticationCallback() {
        override fun onAuthenticationSucceeded(r: BiometricPrompt.AuthenticationResult) {
            unlockUi()
        }
    })
val info = BiometricPrompt.PromptInfo.Builder()
    .setTitle("Unlock your wallet")
    .setNegativeButtonText("Cancel")
    .build()
prompt.authenticate(info)

Policies. .deviceOwnerAuthenticationWithBiometrics allows biometrics only (falls back to nothing; after repeated failures the system locks biometrics until the passcode is entered). .deviceOwnerAuthentication allows biometrics and falls back to the device passcode. Choose the second for most apps so a user with a wet finger is not stuck.

Info.plist. Face ID needs NSFaceIDUsageDescription. Without it, on devices with Face ID, the app crashes or the policy fails; Touch ID needs nothing. Always set it.

Strong way: bind the secret to biometrics. Create the Keychain item with a SecAccessControl so decryption itself requires biometrics. A hacked UI that skips your if success cannot read the secret.

import Security

func biometricProtectedAttributes() -> [String: Any]? {
    var error: Unmanaged<CFError>?
    guard let access = SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags(
        nil,
        kSecAttrAccessibleWhenPasscodeSetThisDeviceOnly,
        .biometryCurrentSet,      // invalidated if fingerprints/face set changes
        &error) else { return nil }
    return [kSecAttrAccessControl as String: access]
}

.biometryCurrentSet invalidates the item when a new face/finger is enrolled, which defeats the attack "attacker knows passcode, enrols own face". .biometryAny survives enrolment changes. Reading the item triggers the system Face ID sheet automatically; pass kSecUseAuthenticationContext with an LAContext to customise the prompt.

Details seniors know.

  • LAContext.biometryType reports .faceID, .touchID, .opticID (Vision Pro) only after calling canEvaluatePolicy.
  • Face ID is not available to apps in the background; evaluation requires the app active.
  • A reused LAContext remembers a successful authentication for touchIDAuthenticationAllowableReuseDuration (maximum limited by the system), which is how "unlock once for several reads" works.
  • Face ID data never leaves the Secure Enclave. Your app only ever gets success or an error code (LAError.userCancel, .biometryLockout, .biometryNotEnrolled, .authenticationFailed).

Real industry examples. Banking apps and password managers (1Password, Bitwarden) offer "unlock with Face ID" and keep the vault key sealed with a biometric-bound access control; the master password is required after N days or after a biometric set change.

Everyday analogy. The weak approach is a guard who says "yes" and you walk through an unlocked door. The strong approach is a safe whose lock itself reads your face.

Common interview traps.

  • Using only evaluatePolicy as the security gate for a secret. It can be bypassed with runtime hooking on a jailbroken phone (Frida); bind to the Keychain instead.
  • Forgetting NSFaceIDUsageDescription.
  • Not handling .biometryLockout and not offering a passcode fallback.
  • Assuming .biometryAny and .biometryCurrentSet behave the same on a new enrolment.

notes.title: The permission model: usage strings and just-in-time prompts
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Android declares <uses-permission> in the manifest and calls requestPermissions (or the Activity Result API); the user can deny and "don't ask again". iOS has no manifest list of permissions. Instead you add a human-readable usage string per capability in Info.plist, and the system prompt appears the first time you touch the API.

Mechanism. The OS owns the decision table per app (TCC, Transparency Consent and Control). The first access shows a prompt using your string. After the user answers, you cannot show the system prompt again. The only route is directing them to Settings. Calling the API after denial just returns "denied"/empty data.

<key>NSCameraUsageDescription</key>
<string>Scan a card so you do not have to type the number.</string>
<key>NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription</key>
<string>Show restaurants near you.</string>
<key>NSMicrophoneUsageDescription</key>
<string>Record voice notes.</string>
<key>NSPhotoLibraryAddUsageDescription</key>
<string>Save the edited picture.</string>

Missing key plus a call to that API means the app is killed instantly (crash log: "This app has crashed because it attempted to access privacy-sensitive data without a usage description"). The App Store also rejects builds (ITMS-90683 "Missing purpose string") that link a framework needing a string you did not provide, even if you never call it.

Just-in-time pattern. Show your own value explanation first (a "pre-prompt"), then trigger the system prompt, because you get exactly one shot.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
import AVFoundation

@MainActor
func ensureCamera() async -> Bool {
    switch AVCaptureDevice.authorizationStatus(for: .video) {
    case .authorized: return true
    case .notDetermined:
        return await AVCaptureDevice.requestAccess(for: .video)
    case .denied, .restricted:
        return false // send to Settings via UIApplication.openSettingsURLString
    @unknown default: return false
    }
}
val launcher = registerForActivityResult(
    ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission()
) { granted -> if (granted) openCamera() else showRationale() }

when {
    ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(this, Manifest.permission.CAMERA)
        == PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED -> openCamera()
    else -> launcher.launch(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)
}

Differences worth memorising.

  • iOS distinguishes .denied (user said no) and .restricted (parental controls / MDM; user cannot change it).
  • Location has "While Using", "Always" and an approximate/precise toggle. Photos has "limited library" in iOS 14+, and PhotosPicker needs no permission at all because it runs out of process.
  • Notifications are not Info.plist-gated; you call UNUserNotificationCenter.requestAuthorization.
  • Android's one-time permission and auto-reset for unused apps have an iOS parallel: location "Allow Once" and periodic reminders for "Always".
  • Android lets you show a rationale after the first denial; iOS gives you no such callback, so detect denial yourself.

Real industry examples. Instagram asks for camera only when you tap the camera, not at launch. Uber shows its own screen explaining why it wants "Always" location before the system dialog. Apps that ask for everything at launch see lower opt-in and risk review rejection under guideline 5.1.1 (data collection and storage) when strings are vague.

Everyday analogy. Think of a doorbell with one ring: you may ring once and the resident answers yes or no forever. You had better say who you are (pre-prompt) before ringing.

Common interview traps.

  • Requesting permissions at launch (low opt-in, review risk).
  • Vague strings like "needed for app features": rejected under 5.1.1.
  • Assuming you can re-prompt after a denial.
  • Forgetting .limited photo authorization or the approximate-location case.

notes.title: Privacy manifests, required reason APIs and App Privacy labels
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Google Play asks you to fill a Data safety form by hand. Apple has two artifacts: App Privacy "nutrition labels" in App Store Connect (manual answers) and a machine-readable PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy file shipped inside your app and inside every third-party SDK.

What the manifest contains. A plist (edit it in Xcode's "App Privacy" editor) with four top-level keys:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>NSPrivacyTracking</key><false/>
  <key>NSPrivacyTrackingDomains</key><array/>
  <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypes</key>
  <array>
    <dict>
      <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataType</key>
      <string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeEmailAddress</string>
      <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeLinked</key><true/>
      <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeTracking</key><false/>
      <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposes</key>
      <array><string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposeAppFunctionality</string></array>
    </dict>
  </array>
  <key>NSPrivacyAccessedAPITypes</key>
  <array>
    <dict>
      <key>NSPrivacyAccessedAPIType</key>
      <string>NSPrivacyAccessedAPICategoryUserDefaults</string>
      <key>NSPrivacyAccessedAPITypeReasons</key>
      <array><string>CA92.1</string></array>
    </dict>
  </array>
</dict>
</plist>

Required reason APIs. Since the May 2024 enforcement, Apple requires a declared approved reason for APIs that are commonly abused for device fingerprinting. The categories: file timestamp APIs (creationDate, stat), system boot time (systemUptime, mach_absolute_time), disk space (volumeAvailableCapacityKey), active keyboard list, and UserDefaults. Reason codes look like CA92.1 (read and write only your own app's defaults). Using one without a declared reason triggers an App Store Connect email (ITMS-91053) and later rejection. Reason codes and exact enforcement dates: verify on developer.apple.com.

Third-party SDKs. Apple published a list of "commonly used SDKs" (Alamofire, Firebase, Kingfisher, SDWebImage, Lottie, and many others) that must ship their own manifest and be code-signed (signature requirement). If a dependency lacks one, bump the version or add a manifest yourself. Xcode can generate an aggregated report: Product > Archive > Generate Privacy Report.

App Privacy labels. Answer in App Store Connect: data types collected (contact info, identifiers, usage data, diagnostics), whether linked to identity, whether used for tracking, and purposes. The labels must match what your SDKs actually do. Crashlytics collects crash data and device identifiers: you must declare diagnostics.

App Tracking Transparency (ATT). Tracking means linking your app's data with third-party data for advertising or sharing with data brokers. If you do that you must call ATTrackingManager.requestTrackingAuthorization and add NSUserTrackingUsageDescription. Without consent, ASIdentifierManager.shared().advertisingIdentifier returns zeros.

import AppTrackingTransparency
import AdSupport

@MainActor
func askForTracking() async {
    // The app must be active, otherwise the prompt silently does not show (verify iOS version behaviour)
    let status = await ATTrackingManager.requestTrackingAuthorization()
    if status == .authorized {
        let idfa = ASIdentifierManager.shared().advertisingIdentifier
        _ = idfa
    }
}
Android iOS
Advertising ID (AAID), user can reset or delete IDFA, off by default until ATT consent
Data safety form App Privacy label + PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy
Settings.Secure.ANDROID_ID identifierForVendor (reset when all your apps are removed)
Play SDK Index Apple's list of commonly used SDKs needing manifests

Real industry examples. After ATT (iOS 14.5, 2021), Meta publicly reported large revenue impact, and mobile attribution moved to SKAdNetwork/AdAttributionKit (verify) and aggregated measurement. Firebase and Adjust ship privacy manifests.

Everyday analogy. The manifest is an ingredients label printed on the box by each supplier; the privacy label is the menu summary the restaurant prints on top. Both must agree with what is in the kitchen.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing ATT is needed for any analytics. It is needed for cross-company tracking; first-party analytics alone does not require it.
  • Forgetting that third-party SDK behaviour counts toward your privacy labels.
  • Using UserDefaults and not declaring the reason: a very common 2024 warning email.
  • Using identifierForVendor as a stable ID across reinstalls; it can change.

notes.title: Data protection classes and file encryption
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Android 10+ uses file-based encryption with credential-encrypted (CE) and device-encrypted (DE) storage. iOS Data Protection is the same idea with four named classes, applied per file.

The classes.

Class Key available Typical content
.complete (NSFileProtectionComplete) only while unlocked health, banking caches
.completeUnlessOpen files already open stay readable after lock in-progress downloads, recordings
.completeUntilFirstUserAuthentication after first unlock since boot (default for new files) most app data
.none always rarely appropriate

Mechanism. Each file has a per-file key wrapped by a class key; class keys are derived from the hardware UID key inside the Secure Enclave plus the user passcode. When the device locks, complete class keys are discarded from memory; reads then fail with errors such as "operation not permitted" / NSFileReadNoPermissionError.

import Foundation

func writeSecret(_ data: Data, to url: URL) throws {
    try data.write(to: url, options: [.atomic, .completeFileProtection])
}

// Exclude a cache from iCloud/iTunes backup
func excludeFromBackup(_ url: URL) throws {
    var url = url
    var values = URLResourceValues()
    values.isExcludedFromBackup = true
    try url.setResourceValues(values)
}

You can also set a default per app through the Data Protection capability (entitlement com.apple.developer.default-data-protection) and for Core Data / SwiftData stores via the store file attributes.

Background pitfall. A complete file read by a background task (silent push, BGTask) while the phone is locked fails. Use completeUntilFirstUserAuthentication for background data and complete only for foreground-only secrets. The symptom in Crashlytics: sporadic SQLite "disk I/O error" (SQLite error 10) or "unable to open database file" mainly for users with locked phones.

Secure Enclave. A separate processor that creates and holds private keys (P-256 only for the direct SecKey API; verify newer CryptoKit curves). You never see the private key, only ask it to sign or key-agree. CryptoKit exposes SecureEnclave.P256.Signing.PrivateKey:

import CryptoKit

func makeEnclaveKey() throws -> SecureEnclave.P256.Signing.PrivateKey {
    guard SecureEnclave.isAvailable else { throw NSError(domain: "se", code: 1) }
    let access = SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags(
        nil, kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly,
        [.privateKeyUsage, .biometryCurrentSet], nil)!
    return try SecureEnclave.P256.Signing.PrivateKey(accessControl: access)
}

SecureEnclave.isAvailable is false in the Simulator; code must branch for it. For ordinary app-level encryption of blobs, use CryptoKit's AES.GCM and store the symmetric key in the Keychain:

import CryptoKit

func encrypt(_ plain: Data, key: SymmetricKey) throws -> Data {
    try AES.GCM.seal(plain, using: key).combined!   // nonce + ciphertext + tag
}
func decrypt(_ blob: Data, key: SymmetricKey) throws -> Data {
    try AES.GCM.open(try AES.GCM.SealedBox(combined: blob), using: key)
}

Real industry examples. Signal encrypts its SQLCipher database and stores the key in the Keychain. Apple Health data sits in class complete. Messaging apps often use completeUntilFirstUserAuthentication so push extensions can decrypt a notification while the phone is locked.

Everyday analogy. Data protection is a diary with a lock whose key is hidden in a drawer that only opens when you are home awake (unlocked); some pages you can still read once you started (completeUnlessOpen).

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing .complete for data touched by notification service extensions or background refresh.
  • Thinking Secure Enclave can store arbitrary data. It stores keys, not blobs.
  • Writing your own crypto (CBC without MAC, reused nonces). Use CryptoKit's AEAD.
  • Forgetting the Simulator has no Secure Enclave.

notes.title: App Transport Security and certificate pinning
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Android's network_security_config.xml blocks cleartext by default from API 28 and lets you pin certificates declaratively. iOS enforces ATS: HTTPS with TLS 1.2+ and forward-secret ciphers for connections made with URLSession (and WebKit) unless you opt out in Info.plist.

ATS rules. Default: require HTTPS, TLS 1.2 minimum, a strong certificate chain. Exceptions live under NSAppTransportSecurity:

<key>NSAppTransportSecurity</key>
<dict>
  <key>NSExceptionDomains</key>
  <dict>
    <key>legacy.example.com</key>
    <dict>
      <key>NSExceptionAllowsInsecureHTTPLoads</key><true/>
    </dict>
  </dict>
</dict>

Avoid NSAllowsArbitraryLoads: App Review asks for a justification and may reject. Prefer per-domain exceptions. Local network development uses NSAllowsLocalNetworking. ATS applies to URLSession, not to raw sockets via Network.framework, which you must secure yourself.

Certificate pinning (what and why). TLS trusts any certificate signed by a CA in the system store. Pinning additionally requires the server's certificate or public key to match a known value, defeating rogue CAs and corporate or malicious proxies (Charles). Two ways:

  1. Pin public key hash (SPKI) in a URLSessionDelegate: survives certificate renewal if the key pair is kept.
  2. Declarative pinning with NSPinnedDomains in Info.plist (iOS 14+), where you list NSPinnedLeafIdentities or NSPinnedCAIdentities as SPKI-SHA256 hashes.
import Foundation
import CryptoKit

final class PinningDelegate: NSObject, URLSessionDelegate, @unchecked Sendable {
    private let pinnedHashes: Set<String>   // base64 SHA-256 of SPKI

    init(pinnedHashes: Set<String>) { self.pinnedHashes = pinnedHashes }

    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession,
                    didReceive challenge: URLAuthenticationChallenge) async
        -> (URLSession.AuthChallengeDisposition, URLCredential?) {
        guard challenge.protectionSpace.authenticationMethod == NSURLAuthenticationMethodServerTrust,
              let trust = challenge.protectionSpace.serverTrust,
              SecTrustEvaluateWithError(trust, nil),                // normal validation first
              let chain = SecTrustCopyCertificateChain(trust) as? [SecCertificate],
              let leaf = chain.first,
              let key = SecCertificateCopyKey(leaf),
              let keyData = SecKeyCopyExternalRepresentation(key, nil) as Data? else {
            return (.cancelAuthenticationChallenge, nil)
        }
        // NOTE: hashing raw key bytes omits the ASN.1 header; real SPKI pinning
        // must prepend the header for the key type (verify; libraries like TrustKit do this).
        let hash = Data(SHA256.hash(data: keyData)).base64EncodedString()
        return pinnedHashes.contains(hash)
            ? (.useCredential, URLCredential(trust: trust))
            : (.cancelAuthenticationChallenge, nil)
    }
}
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
// iOS equivalent with TrustKit/Alamofire ServerTrustManager (library route)
import Alamofire

let evaluators: [String: ServerTrustEvaluating] = [
    "api.example.com": PublicKeysTrustEvaluator()  // pins keys bundled in the app
]
let session = Session(serverTrustManager: ServerTrustManager(evaluators: evaluators))
// Android: OkHttp pinning
val pinner = CertificatePinner.Builder()
    .add("api.example.com", "sha256/AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=")
    .build()
val client = OkHttpClient.Builder().certificatePinner(pinner).build()

Operational risk. Pinning can lock out your whole user base: if the server rotates to a key not in the pin set and users have not updated, every request fails. Ship at least one backup pin, pin the intermediate CA rather than the leaf when possible, and keep a remote kill-switch. Mobile-focused libraries: TrustKit, Alamofire's ServerTrustManager.

Real industry examples. Twitter and banking apps pin; many consumer apps skip it due to operational cost. Google's Chrome dropped HPKP for exactly this lock-out risk. Pen testers bypass pinning on jailbroken devices with SSL Kill Switch or Frida, so pinning raises effort, not impossibility.

Everyday analogy. Ordinary TLS is accepting any ID issued by the national authority. Pinning is saying "I only open the door to this one named person whose photo I already have". If that person changes their face, nobody gets in.

Common interview traps.

  • Flipping NSAllowsArbitraryLoads to "fix" a dev problem and shipping it.
  • Pinning the leaf certificate with no backup, then rotating it.
  • Writing a delegate that returns .useCredential without evaluating the trust (a classic vulnerability).
  • Thinking ATS governs WKWebView JS or Network.framework raw sockets in the same way.

notes.title: Secure coding for network and storage
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. The same OWASP Mobile hygiene as on Android: no secrets in the binary, validate server input, avoid logging PII. The iOS-specific parts are the places data leaks: pasteboard, screenshots, URL schemes, logs and backups.

Practical checklist with code.

  1. Secrets in the app binary are public. strings on the IPA reveals API keys in Swift code or plists. Put real secrets on a backend; use a short-lived token. For build-time config use .xcconfig files (not committed) which inject Info.plist values; for third-party keys that must ship, treat them as public and restrict them server-side.
# Config.xcconfig (gitignored)
API_BASE_URL = https:/$()/api.example.com
  1. Hide content in the app switcher. iOS snapshots your UI when you background. Cover sensitive screens.
import SwiftUI

struct PrivacyShield: ViewModifier {
    @Environment(\.scenePhase) private var phase
    func body(content: Content) -> some View {
        content.overlay {
            if phase != .active { Color.black.ignoresSafeArea() }
        }
    }
}
  1. Pasteboard. UIPasteboard.general is readable by other apps (iOS 14+ shows a banner when an app reads it; iOS 16 adds a paste prompt). Mark secrets as local-only and expiring: UIPasteboard.general.setItems([[...]], options: [.localOnly: true, .expirationDate: Date().addingTimeInterval(60)]).
  2. Logging. os.Logger privacy: interpolations are private (redacted) by default in release for dynamic strings; mark values explicitly with privacy: .private or .public. print in release is a leak path and costs performance.
import os
let log = Logger(subsystem: "com.example.app", category: "auth")
log.info("login for \(email, privacy: .private(mask: .hash))")
  1. Deep links and URL schemes. Custom schemes (myapp://) can be claimed by any app. Prefer Universal Links (associated domains + apple-app-site-association) and treat all link parameters as untrusted input.
  2. WebViews. Disable javaScriptCanOpenWindowsAutomatically if unused, whitelist navigation in WKNavigationDelegate, and never expose a message handler that executes arbitrary native actions.
  3. Backups and SQLite. Excluding secrets from backup via ...ThisDeviceOnly Keychain items and isExcludedFromBackup files.
  4. Sign in. Use ASWebAuthenticationSession (shared Safari cookies, no credential-stealing embedded web view) for OAuth, and PKCE. Passkeys via AuthenticationServices are the modern replacement for passwords.

Real industry examples. Banking apps blank the app switcher snapshot; Apple's own Wallet does too. Several apps were reported reading the clipboard on every launch after iOS 14's paste banner exposed the behaviour (TikTok, LinkedIn and others publicly), a reminder to read the pasteboard only on user action.

Everyday analogy. Leaking data is like leaving documents on the bus: not the safe that failed, but the pasteboard (shared desk), screenshots (photo copier) and logs (diary left open).

Common interview traps.

  • Embedding a Stripe secret or OpenAI key in the app because "it is obfuscated".
  • Logging tokens with print/NSLog (visible in the Console app and sysdiagnose).
  • Using custom URL schemes to pass auth codes.
  • Using UIWebView-style embedded login instead of ASWebAuthenticationSession.

notes.title: Jailbreak detection, obfuscation limits and MASVS
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Root detection and Play Integrity on Android; on iOS jailbreak detection plus App Attest. In both worlds the app runs on a device the attacker controls, so client-side checks are advisory only.

Common jailbreak signals (all bypassable):

  • Presence of files: /Applications/Cydia.app, /bin/bash, /usr/sbin/sshd, /etc/apt.
  • Ability to write outside the sandbox (writing to /private/test.txt succeeds).
  • Ability to call fork() successfully (sandboxed apps cannot).
  • Suspicious dynamic libraries loaded (MobileSubstrate, FridaGadget) via _dyld_image_count.
  • Custom URL schemes such as cydia:// returning canOpenURL true (requires the scheme in LSApplicationQueriesSchemes).
  • A debugger attached (sysctl with P_TRACED flag), or ptrace(PT_DENY_ATTACH) to hinder it.
import Foundation

func looksJailbroken() -> Bool {
    #if targetEnvironment(simulator)
    return false
    #else
    let paths = ["/Applications/Cydia.app", "/usr/sbin/sshd", "/etc/apt", "/bin/bash"]
    if paths.contains(where: { FileManager.default.fileExists(atPath: $0) }) { return true }
    let probe = "/private/jb_probe.txt"
    if (try? "x".write(toFile: probe, atomically: true, encoding: .utf8)) != nil {
        try? FileManager.default.removeItem(atPath: probe)
        return true
    }
    return false
    #endif
}

Honest limits. A determined attacker hooks the check with Frida/Objection or uses a rootless jailbreak that hides the files; checks only deter casual cheaters. Move the real decision to the server: App Attest (DCAppAttestService) produces a hardware-backed assertion that the request came from a genuine, unmodified build of your app on real Apple hardware; your backend verifies it. DeviceCheck gives two bits per device on Apple's servers (e.g. "already claimed free trial"). Both are server-validated. Availability of App Attest on all device types: verify.

Obfuscation and binary hardening. Swift has name mangling, not obfuscation, and class-dump-style tools (and Hopper/Ghidra) still recover logic. Commercial tools (Guardsquare iXGuard, Appdome) add string encryption and control-flow obfuscation. Bitcode (which allowed Apple-side processing) was removed in Xcode 14. Worthwhile steps: strip symbols in release (Strip Linked Product), enable PIE and stack protectors (defaults), disable debug logging, and keep secrets off the device. Android R8 shrinking has no direct iOS twin; release builds in Swift with whole-module optimisation already inline heavily.

OWASP MASVS. The Mobile Application Security Verification Standard (v2) has control groups: STORAGE, CRYPTO, AUTH, NETWORK, PLATFORM, CODE, RESILIENCE, PRIVACY. The companion MASTG gives test procedures, and the levels (L1 standard, L2 defence-in-depth, R resilience) tell you how much to invest. Interview framing: L1 for every app, L2 plus R for banking and payments. Exact group names in the latest version: verify.

Real industry examples. Pokemon Go and banking apps refuse to run on jailbroken devices; Niantic's checks were repeatedly bypassed within days. Pen-test houses use MobSF, Frida, Objection and Burp to test apps against MASTG.

Everyday analogy. Jailbreak detection is a bouncer checking for a suspicious bulge in your coat; a determined guest simply wears a different coat. App Attest is a notarised letter that the venue can verify with the notary itself.

Common interview traps.

  • Presenting jailbreak detection as sufficient protection; the answer is "defence in depth with server checks".
  • Calling Swift "unreadable so it is secure".
  • Treating DeviceCheck/App Attest as client-side features; verification happens on the server.
  • Forgetting the Simulator branch so checks misfire during development.

notes.title: Putting it together: a secure session flow
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. On Android you would combine EncryptedSharedPreferences, BiometricPrompt with a CryptoObject, and OkHttp pinning. The iOS recipe uses the same pieces under different names.

Login (ASWebAuthenticationSession + PKCE)
   -> access token (short-lived, memory) + refresh token
   -> refresh token in Keychain: AfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly
   -> optional "high-value" secret: biometryCurrentSet access control
   -> every request: URLSession (ATS + pinning delegate)
   -> sensitive screens: privacy shield in app switcher
   -> backend: verifies App Attest assertion on risky calls

An end-to-end sketch combining the earlier snippets:

import Foundation

actor SessionStore {
    private let keychain = Keychain(service: "com.example.app.session")
    private var accessToken: String?

    func refreshToken() throws -> String {
        let data = try keychain.load(account: "refresh")
        return String(decoding: data, as: UTF8.self)
    }

    func store(access: String, refresh: String) throws {
        accessToken = access                       // memory only
        try keychain.save(Data(refresh.utf8), account: "refresh")
    }

    func signOut() {
        accessToken = nil
        // delete keychain item with SecItemDelete (omitted for brevity)
    }
}

An actor gives data-race safety under Swift 6 strict concurrency, and Keychain is Sendable because it holds only a let string.

Incident patterns to recognise.

  • Users logged out randomly after a restore: the Keychain used ThisDeviceOnly and they migrated phones. Expected; handle by re-auth.
  • Background refresh failing for locked phones: wrong accessibility class (errSecInteractionNotAllowed).
  • App rejected for ITMS-90683 missing purpose string after adding an SDK.
  • Mass network failure after certificate rotation with pinning and no backup pin.
  • Review rejection for 5.1.1 because the camera string said only "Camera access".

Real industry examples. Auth0, Okta and Firebase mobile guides all recommend: PKCE, refresh tokens in the Keychain, short-lived access tokens. Apple's own sample code "Protecting keys with the Secure Enclave" demonstrates the key-in-hardware pattern.

Everyday analogy. A secure session is a hotel stay: a keycard (short-lived access token) opens your room, the front desk (Keychain) holds your reservation (refresh token), and the lobby cameras (App Attest on the server) confirm you are the guest.

Common interview traps.

  • Persisting the access token and refresh token in the same insecure place.
  • Forgetting sign-out must clear the Keychain items and caches.
  • Answering with tools but no threat model; start from "what is the attacker able to do".

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• iOS security rests on sandboxing, code signing, entitlements and OS-level consent; the Keychain replaces Android Keystore-based storage.
  • Use the Keychain for secrets, with AfterFirstUnlock for background-readable tokens and ThisDeviceOnly for non-migrating ones; remember items survive uninstall.
  • LAContext alone is a UI gate; bind secrets to SecAccessControl with biometrics (biometryCurrentSet) and always set NSFaceIDUsageDescription.
  • Permissions are per-capability Info.plist usage strings with one-shot system prompts; ask just in time and handle .denied/.restricted/.limited.
  • Privacy manifests, required reason APIs (including UserDefaults), SDK manifests and App Privacy labels are enforced at upload; ATT is required for cross-company tracking only.
  • Data protection classes govern file readability while locked; choose completeUntilFirstUserAuthentication for anything background code touches; Secure Enclave holds keys only.
  • ATS enforces HTTPS; pin with backup pins or NSPinnedDomains, never ship NSAllowsArbitraryLoads, never return .useCredential without evaluating trust.
  • Jailbreak checks and obfuscation only deter; real trust decisions belong on the server (App Attest, DeviceCheck), measured against OWASP MASVS levels.
